Text: When approaching a potentially hostile patient, do not take an aggressive posture such as {{c1::crossing your arms}}, {{c1::clenching your fists}}, or {{c1::placing your hands on your hips}}; instead stand with your {{c2::palms facing out}}.
Back Extra:
Why: an aggressive posture signals impatience or a claim of authority, while open palms communicate openness and acceptance and allow for quick movement if needed.

Pitfall: personal safety is your primary concern with a hostile patient, so first assess scene safety and consider law enforcement and backup.

Text: With a potentially hostile patient you should make {{c1::good eye contact, but not stare}}, and speak {{c2::calmly, confidently, and slowly}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a steady but non-fixed gaze and a calm, slow voice help de-escalate without appearing to challenge the patient.

Pitfall: never threaten the patient verbally or physically; personal safety is the primary concern.

Text: You arrive to find an agitated man pacing and shouting. To help de-escalate, you keep your {{c1::palms facing out}} and avoid {{c2::crossing your arms}}. What tone and pace should your voice have? {{c3::calm, confident, and slow::manner}}
Back Extra:
Cue: open palms plus a calm, slow voice reads as non-threatening and leaves room for quick movement.

Pitfall: assess scene safety and get law enforcement or backup before closing distance; never threaten the patient.

Text: An {{c1::open-ended::type}} question is one the patient must answer with {{c2::some level of detail}}, whereas a {{c3::closed-ended::type}} question can be answered in a {{c4::short or single-word}} response.
Back Extra:
Ex: open-ended = "What seems to be bothering you today?"; closed-ended = "Are you having chest pain?"

Distinguish: open-ended questions let the conversation flow and the patient direct you; closed-ended questions yield limited information and are only a starting point.

Text: When first approaching a patient you should use {{c1::open-ended::open/closed}} questions, but switch to {{c2::closed-ended::open/closed}} questions when the patient cannot give long or complete answers.
Back Extra:
Why: open-ended questions let the patient direct you to the problem; a patient in severe respiratory distress or a young child may only manage short answers.

Pitfall: closed-ended answers give limited information, so treat them as only a starting point.

Text: Before beginning the patient interview, you and your partner should determine {{c1::which provider will lead}} the interview.
Back Extra: Why: deciding the lead ensures you do not ask questions at the same time or ask repetitive questions.

Text: To avoid confusing the patient (who may just answer "yes"), it is best to ask a {{c1::single question}}, wait for an answer, and then proceed to the next question.
Back Extra: Pitfall: asking two questions at once, such as one open-ended and one closed-ended together, often gets a single "yes" that answers neither clearly.

Text: In therapeutic communication, {{c1::reflection::technique}} is restating a patient's statement back to them to confirm your understanding.
Back Extra:
Ex: Patient: "I am so depressed I could die." EMT: "I understand you are feeling depressed."

Distinguish: reflection mirrors what the patient said; clarification instead asks the patient to explain what they meant.

Text: In therapeutic communication, {{c1::clarification::technique}} is asking the patient to explain what he or she meant by an answer.
Back Extra:
Ex: EMT: "When you say you feel 'funny,' can you tell me exactly what that feels like?"

Distinguish: clarification asks the patient to explain further; reflection restates what the patient already said to confirm you understood it.

Text: The therapeutic communication technique of {{c1::confrontation::technique}} is used to make a patient who is in denial or in a state of shock focus on urgent, life-critical issues.
Back Extra:
Ex: firmly redirecting a patient who insists he is "fine" to let you control the heavy bleeding from his arm.

Distinguish: confrontation redirects a resistant patient to the critical problem; facilitation simply encourages a willing patient to keep talking.

Text: The therapeutic communication technique of {{c1::facilitation::technique}} means encouraging the patient to talk more or provide more information.
Back Extra:
Ex: EMT: "I am listening. Can you tell me more about that?"

Distinguish: facilitation draws out more from a willing patient; interpretation instead restates the patient's complaint to confirm your understanding of it.

Text: During a patient interview you should avoid giving {{c1::false hope or reassurance}}, because {{c2::you do not actually know that everything will be okay}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: promising a good outcome you cannot guarantee can destroy trust when it proves untrue.

Text: During a patient interview you should avoid {{c1::"why" questions}}, because they {{c2::appear to accuse the listener}}.
Back Extra: Ex: "Why did you stop taking your medication?" sounds accusatory; "What made it hard to keep taking it?" does not.

Text: During a patient interview you should avoid speaking in {{c1::professional jargon}}, because it {{c2::confuses the patient}}.
Back Extra: Why: most patients do not understand medical jargon, so plain language keeps communication open.
